content.text: *Functional Incontinence: due to physical or cognitive disability (delirium, dementia) w/ a normal GU system
Involuntary urinary leakage preceded by or accompanied by sudden urge to urinate
: detrusor muscle is stimulated by muscarinic acetylcholine receptors –
overactivity leads to uninhibited (involuntary) detrusor muscle contractions during bladder filling
: increased age, idiopathic, bladder infection (cystitis), stones or tumor
increased urgency, frequency, small volume voids, nocturia
w/ an inability to make it to the bathroom in time
– timed frequent voiding, using a voiding diary to identify the shortest voiding intervals, decreased fluid intake
: avoid spicy foods, citrus fruit, chocolate, alcohol, & caffeine
– beta-3 agonist that causes bladder relaxation
– central & peripheral anticholinergic effect & alpha-adrenergic agonist (
bladder muscle relaxation, ↑ bladder outlet resistance, antispasmodic effect on detrusor muscle, ↑ urethral sphincter tone
Urinary retention & incomplete bladder emptying leads to involuntary urine leakage once the bladder is full (aka it overflows)
MC in neurological disorders or autonomic dysfunction
– DM, multiple sclerosis, spinal injuries, spinal stenosis, peripheral neuropathy associated w/ vitamin B12 deficiency
, uterine fibroids, pelvic organ prolapse, overcorrection of urethra from prior pelvic floor surgery
loss of urine w/ no warning (as in urge) or triggers (as in stress)
leakage or dribbling in the setting of incomplete bladder emptying, weak or intermittent urinary stream, hesitancy, frequency, nocturia
– leakage often occurs w/ changes in position
•Urodynamic testing to differentiate it from urethral obstruction in men
intermittent or indwelling catheterization first line
Involuntary leakage of urine that occurs once ↑ abdominal pressure (e.g., exertion, coughing, laughing, sneezing) is greater than urethral pressure & resistance or urine flow
MC type of incontinence in younger women
(e.g., childbirth, surgery, postmenopausal estrogen loss) – although rare in men,
may be associated w/ stress incontinence
– insufficient support from the pelvic floor musculature & the vaginal connective tissue to the urethra & bladder neck
•Cystoscopy and urodynamic testing to evaluate function
urine leakage during times of increased intra-abdominal pressure
(e.g., coughing, laughing, sneezing, lifting heavy objects) –
there is NO urge to urinate prior to leakage
– initial treatment of choice; Kegel supportive therapy includes supervised therapy, vaginal weighted cones or biofeedback; bladder training (e.g., timed voidings);
topical estrogen for postmenopausal women w/ vaginal atrophy
– used in conjunction w/ pelvic floor exercises; protective garments & pads, weight loss, smoking cessation, & drinking smaller amounts of water throughout the day
– used if incomplete efficacy w/ lifestyle modifications & muscle strengthening or situational stress incontinence
(higher success rates than conservative therapy); more rapid & definitive tx
